Title: IRS official who refused to testify facing more scrutiny over scandal, past
Summary:
The IRS official who refused to testify at a House hearing Wednesday has become a key focus of the congressional investigations into the IRS practice of singling out conservative groups. Now under the protection of her lawyers and the Fifth Amendment, Lois Lerner is facing a maelstrom of controversy.
Members of Congress are calling her evasive, and question why she didn't reveal the program sooner -- plus her history at the Federal Elections Commission is coming under scrutiny.
Lerner touched off the public controversy when, at an American Bar Association conference earlier this month, she apologized for the IRS' practice of targeting conservative organizations for additional scrutiny. It was the first time the agency acknowledged the practice.
"They used names like Tea Party or patriots... and they selected cases simply because the application had those names in the title," she admitted.
She said she hadn't revealed the information sooner, because she was never asked. But just two days before the ABA conference, Lerner was specifically asked about the investigation.
Rep. Joseph Crowley, D-N.Y., asked her if she could "comment briefly on the status on the IRS investigation into these political not-for-profits."
She said: "There's a questionnaire that began this discussion and there's also a questionnaire out there that is seeking info from 501 c3,4,5 organizations."
Crowley later called her answer evasive.
"The bottom line is you cannot lie to Congress, and you cannot be evasive, you cannot try to mislead Congress," he said.
In the 1990's, Lerner also served as chief of enforcement at the Federal Elections Commission.
Under her direction, the FEC undertook the largest enforcement action in its history -- suing the Christian Coalition for violating campaign laws. The Christian Coalition won, but in one deposition, FEC lawyers asked a defendant if televangelist Pat Robertson prayed for him.
James Bopp, the Christian Coalition's lawyer, said he was "shocked and appalled" by that.
"Both political activity and religious activity are specifically protected by the First Amendment," he said.
When Bopp learned years later that Lerner had been promoted to an IRS position, he became concerned.
"She was in effect being promoted for what she had done at the Federal Election Commission and now was going to be expected... to replicate that at the IRS and now we know that's exactly what happened," he said.

They also made it clear that while the Obama administration has not yet formally acknowledged the existence of a “secret program” called Prism, it has been in the works for more than a year.
This was no longer a secret, Mr. Clapper said, but now an official, government system of intelligence analysis that involves hundreds of companies that have made public statements to the effect that they do not give the government information on the servers that handle Internet information.
“The nature of the government’s activities may still be ‘secret law’ in certain instances,” Mr. Clapper said. “But there is no longer a ‘secret’ program called Prism, and the programs that are now being disclosed do not involve a ‘secret’ database.”
The Justice Department and the F.B.I. are seeking to limit the ability of those companies to give the public the impression that they have not handed over data under court order. The Internal Revenue Service announced Thursday that the IRS has made a final decision on a rule that the agency previously issued to allow couples to claim married filing jointly status. The IRS will no longer automatically accept a joint tax return when a couple's income exceeds certain thresholds, the agency said in a notice to the Internal Revenue Service public address system.

In a separate announcement, Treasury said that because the ruling does not apply to domestic partnerships and civil unions, the IRS will continue to treat same-sex couples differently from other married couples, such as opposite-sex married couples and civil unions.
"We believe these changes are consistent with the law and are in the best interests of our nation. As an example, the tax treatment of married people with same-sex partners is inconsistent with other marriage equality rulings," Treasury Secretary Jacob Lew said in a written statement. "This decision will enhance the tax treatment of married same-sex couples. It will not change the IRS's current treatment of opposite-sex married couples and civil unions. Taxpayers need certainty about their tax law and they deserve it."
The decision is not final and the IRS may request revisions.

Colorado has raised more than $60 million from marijuana sales and taxes, but it needs money to hire more police and staff to make arrests for possession, impound and seize vehicles that have been seized by local police departments and other agencies due to marijuana possession.
Suthers said he was unaware of the lawsuit and the other states’ lawsuit against Colorado before issuing a policy statement in May that said Colorado pot is legal for adults under 21.
He said the measure is legal because it was passed by voters but not enforced because state police don’t have the resources.
"We cannot begin enforcement with just the federal government's inaction,” Suthers said. "We are responsible for ensuring that our state remains the safest in the nation."

"We cannot begin enforcement with just the federal government's inaction," he said. "We are responsible for ensuring that our state remains the safest in the nation."

The two states said they want the U.S. Supreme Court to void parts of Amendment 64, which was approved by voters in November. The measure legalized marijuana for adults over the age of 21, but prohibited its use or possession by minors.

The suit by Nebraska and Oklahoma alleges that Colorado had failed to address marijuana use and sales as required by federal law. It says Colorado “took action, however, that allowed the cannabis flow from the gap in the federal law into neighboring states — in violation of federal law.”
The suit also argues that the Supreme Court should strike down Colorado’s system of retail marijuana sales and taxation, which was upheld by the United States Supreme Court in 2012. The suit points to a federal statute that says the sale and taxation of retail marijuana would violate federal law, saying “such a scheme would subject states to the risk of being subject to federal sanctions.”
Colorado does have regulations that regulate marijuana sales, such as requiring a government-issued identification card for those buying from an Illinois-licensed store. Title: Arkansas Gov. Signs Amended Religious Freedom Bill
Summary:
The Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), signed into law in 2005, seeks to allow certain types of religious groups to refuse to serve LGBT individuals for sincerely held religious beliefs. Those groups that are not allowed to do so must be subject to government scrutiny and may be subject to civil liability. A new bill in Arkansas has been filed that seeks to expand the scope of the law to include gender identity and sexual orientation, in particular.

Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson (R) signed a revised version of the state's Religious Freedom Reformation Act on Thursday, one day after refusing to sign an earlier version of the bill over concerns about discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender individuals.
Earlier Thursday, the Republican-controlled state legislature passed a new version of the bill at the governor's request, amending provisions that would have allowed businesses to discriminate against LGBT customers. The amended legislation mirrors the federal RFRA.
Meanwhile, legislators in Indiana have made changes to the controversial RFRA signed into law by Gov. Mike Pence (R) last week. On Thursday, the state's general assembly passed new language explicitly stating that the law does not allow discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The changes came amid immense national backlash, with dozens of politicians, business leaders and celebrities speaking out against the bill.
In a Wednesday press conference announcing his opposition to the initial version of the bill, Hutchinson said his son had asked him to veto the legislation.
"My son Seth signed the petition asking me, Dad, the governor, to veto this bill," he said. "And he gave me permission to make that reference, and it shows that families -- and there's a generational difference of opinion on these issues."
Hutchinson also faced pressure from Walmart, which is headquartered in the state. CEO Doug McMillon called on the governor to veto the bill, which he said "threatens to undermine the spirit of inclusion."

Title: Arkansas Gov. Signs Amended Religious Freedom Bill
Summary:
The Religious Freedom Reformation Act of 2017 was signed into law today by Governor Hutchinson (R).

Arkansas Governor Asa Hutchinson (R), Arkansas's Republican governor, was one of the first states to sign an RFRA in the nation.
In doing so, he took some controversial stands that were not popular among the state's conservative members of Congress, which was part of a larger push by GOP legislators to pass a revised law.
The law mirrors the federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act which was passed by Congress in 1993. In the states that have adopted it, businesses that wish to deny employees or applicants the right to exercise their religious beliefs may be sued for damages.
Hutchinson said in a press release that he supports the need for the law because it is in line with his conservative beliefs, but that he will continue the "tough and comprehensive" approach taken by Arkansas officials, even though he will be forced to sign the new bill again.
"I do recognize that the original RFRA has not been in the best interests of Arkansas," Hutchinson said. "But it is a better bill than the one I am not signing."
Hutchinson signed the new law Friday morning, the first major step towards reopening the state's economy.
The governor also signed a revised version of the bill, which provides protections for religious groups from being forced to accept employees or applicants from "non-religious" groups or entities. That law will go into effect next year and will be fully enforced beginning in 2019.
At least one Republican lawmaker had expressed some concerns about the law, saying it didn't offer many protections.
The initial version of the bill had a religious liberty clause that allowed businesses to deny employment to people who were not of their faith and "who engaged in conduct that in fact violated the sincerely held religious beliefs of an objecting individual."
The new version says that businesses can no longer discriminate based on sexual orientation or gender identity.
"The governor has been clear that in his administration he will enforce the new law and he will continue to make the tough decisions necessary to ensure the well-being of those who have already signed, while also protecting Arkansas' economy and people," said Arkansas Attorney General Dustin McDaniel.
The Arkansas legislature has also passed language which declares the Religious Freedom Restoration Act to be constitutional.
But a judge in December temporarily blocked the measure from going into effect. The Arkansas Department of Health was also reportedly considering its lawsuit against the law's provisions.

Title: Indiana Governor Says Legislators May Clarify Religious Beliefs Law
Summary:
Gov. Mike Pence of Indiana, seeking to improve a controversial new religious freedom law, signed a compromise law that bars discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.
He said in a statement: “The Indiana Religious Freedom Restoration Act is a good step toward protecting the religious freedom of Indiana’s business community by providing the governor with the tools he needs to protect Indiana businesses from the harmful effects of anti-religious discrimination.”
He added, “This is another strong step to improve our state and help protect religious freedom in Indiana.”
The governor signed the measure into law in a signing statement that was read by state senator Tom Niehaus, a Democrat.
The law takes effect July 1, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of religious belief or practice among “those engaged in the practice of religion.” The measure also clarifies that the state’s public schools can discriminate against gay and lesbian students, the statement said.
State legislators passed the bill unanimously after a months-long debate.
The new law was signed by Mr. Pence, a former state senator, who is a conservative Republican and chairman of the House Budget Committee. Mr. Pence also signed a separate bill extending health benefits for religious leaders who refuse to serve gay and lesbian employees or to provide services that violate their religious beliefs.

Huckabee already stands at the head of the pack for some of the most conservative evangelical leaders in the country, and his entrance into the race could serve to unify the religious right in his party for the next few months, until his next opportunity arises to challenge a national political figure.
Huckabee said he would likely campaign across the country over the next few months to meet with as many local conservative activists as possible. Then he would focus solely on a national political race.

Summary:

He said he is willing to negotiate with Congress but only if Congress agrees to fast-track the entire trade agenda. Title: Arkansas governor seeks changes in religious freedom bill
Summary:
The Arkansas Legislature was scheduled to meet Thursday to discuss a revised version of a religious freedom bill that would allow businesses and individuals to discriminate based on sexual orientation. The revised bill was unanimously passed out of the house Tuesday night on a 31 to 2 vote, and Senate passage on a 24 to 3 vote Thursday. If signed into law by Hutchinson, the state would become the 18th state to enact a law like the one currently in effect in Indiana.
The Arkansas bill would prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, as well as for employment. Under the current state law, businesses and individuals could still opt to prohibit religious beliefs based on sexual orientation if they don't promote or endorse it or its expression, or if they don't have a compelling interest, including a sincerely held religious belief that a significant change to that belief is required in order to conform to their religious community's norms. The Arkansas law includes similar language.
Gov. Hutchinson said the bill strikes a "good balance." He said he wants to "correct" the wording and "make some changes" in the legislation so it better mirrors the federal law.
"This is a bill we could sign as is and maybe change this bill in other ways," he said. "The intent was to give citizens the flexibility to be able to exercise their religion, and it's got a lot of unintended consequences that really we are seeking to remedy today."
The bill has come under fire because it includes language similar to a federal law known as the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA), which prohibits government and nonprofit institutions that receive public assistance from discriminating against someone on the basis of their sexual orientation or gender identity. The federal law, called DOMA, prohibits such discrimination in the name of religion or conscience. In July, U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts said the federal law "may cause the kind of confusion" the court previously said was acceptable under the U.S. Constitution.
Pending the Arkansas law's approval, Hutchinson said he has made some "corrections" to the federal legislation that address the "generational gap" and the issue of tolerance. But he reiterated he is still open to changing the bill to better reflect the 1993 federal law and other laws passed in other states. Hutchinson said he will take a look at the law and consider his options, but he declined to make any other comments at the press conference.

Summary:
The backlash to Indiana's new religious freedom law grew Monday, even as state lawmakers move to clarify the legislation, with Wash. Gov. Jay Inslee and Seattle Mayor Ed Murray banning government-funded travel to Indiana.

The statements are the latest boycott threats to emerge over claims that the law has the potential to discriminate against gays and others.

Murray, a Democrat who is openly gay, issued his ban via executive order over the weekend, and Inslee issued his Monday afternoon.

"I find Indiana's new law disturbing, particularly at a time when more and more states and people in America are embracing civil rights for everyone," Inslee said in a statement. "Washington will join other states and cities in opposing this law and I will impose an administration-wide ban on state-funded travel to Indiana."

Murray says the law doesn't reflect Seattle residents' values. He also has told all city departments to review their contracts to see whether Seattle is doing business with any company whose headquarters is in Indiana.

"Seattleites know that discrimination has no place in our city," he said in a statement. "That’s just equality 101."

The primary concern is that the law might allow a business to discriminate against gay residents, such as a baker being allowed refuse an order from a gay couple for a wedding cake.

But state lawmakers and Republican Gov. Mike Pence have been defending and trying to explain the Religious Freedom Restoration Act ever since the governor signed it into law on Thursday. They note that then-President Bill Clinton in 1993 signed similar federal legislation into law, and 19 other states also have similar policies.

However, the Indiana law differs in several ways, primarily in that it allows a business to assert a right to "the free exercise of religion."

On Monday, state Senate President Pro Tem David Long and House Speaker Brian Bosma, both Republicans, held a press conference to further explain the law. They said they will swiftly try to "clarify" its language.

"The new law does not discriminate," Long said. "And it will not be allowed. To the extent that we need to clarify through legislative action, we plan to do just that.”

Title: Ryan facing Catholic prof complaints over budget comments ahead of Georgetown speech
Summary:
GOP Rep. Paul Ryan is now preparing a speech in Georgetown, but not before a Catholic school knuckle-rapping.
By Paul Kane and The Washington Post
The Rev. Al Joffe of St. Joseph Church in Chicago is the speaker of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Budget and Fiscal Policy Committee this week.
At the session, Joffe said “I'm happy to come” to hear Ryan speak. But he made it clear the Catholic prelate is not coming to the committee’s Washington hotel for an easy ride.
“The budget committee is going to be dealing with many aspects of it,” he said, including how to pay for entitlements and what to do about the national debt. “I hope we're going to hear a balanced message on those topics.”
Joffe added that he was happy to see Ryan attend the conference because of “the seriousness of the issues.”
“I hope the Catholic bishops are not just going to say, ‘You can do this’ and ‘You can do that.’ I'm happy to see that. It's all about the principles,” he said.
The budget deal reached by House Republicans last month was a compromise to the GOP’s failure to tackle the deficit, which was $1 trillion above its current budget, and the debt.
The House budget plan was supposed to cut $1.5 trillion from the federal budget and add $2 trillion to the economy over 10 years.
The fiscal commission report last week, which warned of massive damage to the nation’s economy if the proposal didn’t go through, says Ryan may not have enough votes to pass his budget through.
Joffe also defended Ryan as a “good communicator” and an “effective budget manager.”
“He's got a good sense of what to do on Capitol Hill and how to take a compromise,” Joffe said. “He knows his budget is in order.”
The Wisconsin congressman, who has said he won't discuss the budget until after his speech to Georgetown, is heading to Georgetown in the afternoon.
But his speech will not be an easy one.
Ryan, a Catholic, has made it clear that he plans to talk about the importance of the Christian view of subsidiarity, saying it’s central to fiscal policy.

Summary:
Despite his support for traditional marriage and a strong desire to avoid what he considers an “assault on the institution”, Cathy has come under fire from the right in the past few days over comments he made in an interview with the Washington Post this week. Among other things, Cathy says he supports civil unions between two men and women, but prefers “spousal” marriages between men and women. He calls for a national recognition of same-sex marriages. And he believes that the Bible’s teaching on the “biblical family” includes same-sex marriages. All of which is to say, conservatives have been raving about Chick-fil-A for a while. But there’s no doubt now that this may have an outsized effect.
Chick-fil-A supporters have been busy. In early March, they started an online petition to get Cathy to make a public apology for his remarks on marriage. The petition has received over 300,000 signatures, and the National Gay and Lesbian Task Force has joined in to help make sure the public debate gets to Cathy and his corporate headquarters.
A number of conservatives have been taking a shot at Chick-fil-A for years, from the right and left. The gay advocacy group Alliance Defending Freedom – run by one of the GOP’s most controversial members, the ex-congressman and ex-New York mayor Rudy Giuliani – has sued Chick-fil-A over the years in an attempt to end the fast-food chain’s support for the Traditional Values Coalition, a coalition of conservative evangelical organizations that has been among the most influential organizations in the movement to fight gay marriage and other issues related to traditional marriage. And even before that, Chick-fil-A has been in hot water for opposing the Equal Rights Amendment – an effort by states to amend the U.S. Constitution to define marriage as the union of one man and one woman.
Still, Chick-fil-A has done very little to address critics of its gay marriage stance. It’s still listed on Chick-fil-A’s annual “Top 10” list of “Best Companies” in America – but no CEO has ever apologized publicly for its support of traditional marriage. And it hasn’t apologized for an attempt at a nationwide prayer breakfast. Cathy has also tried to distance himself from WinShape, the charity run by his brother, Jim, a former CEO of Chick-fil-A.

Title: Obama Boehner Fiscal Cliff Meeting: Grasping For Last-Minute Solution
Summary:
President Obama and House Speaker John Boehner met on Thursday for a 90-minute meeting with no word on a deal.
Key details:
The president and Boehner did not exchange pleasantries, and they avoided any discussion about tax hikes, tax cuts, or the need for a new debt ceiling. Instead, they agreed to meet again on January 2.
“We came out here today to talk to each other and to get to know each other on a personal level,” Boehner said at the meeting, CNN’s Carol Costello tweeted from the White House. “I appreciate the president’s desire to get to know him personally, and that he wants to do the right thing.”

The president and his staff may not be in the mood to engage in polite conversation, but they certainly aren't shy about meeting heads-on to discuss issues.
Aides said the meeting was productive and focused. It is now a matter of waiting until January to see if the president comes to his senses, or if he continues to insist on a series of tax hikes and spending cuts that could be difficult to reconcile with the nation's long-term fiscal path.
Obama and Boehner’s meeting was part of an informal White House policy of reaching out to the GOP to improve prospects for a deal that doesn't add to the debt, but puts the country in fiscal crisis.
The president said the president's expectation is to bring a new revenue source -- possibly a new entitlement program -- and make sure that government is not going off the fiscal cliff, which would put the country on a path to a debt limit increase as soon as Congress fails to do its job, officials said.

Summary:
The two-week standoff between Republicans and the Obama administration came to a head on Monday with the release of a bipartisan report from the Joint Committee on Taxation and the Treasury Department that included estimates on tax hikes and spending reductions for the fiscal year that ends September 30.
The committee’s recommendations — which have yet to be approved by the president and Congress — were met with a chorus of objections from the White House. At a House press conference on Monday, the president cast the report as “the latest in a long line of political gimmicks” that would drive up federal deficits and make the U.S. less competitive in the global marketplace.
Later on Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said that “we know there is going to be a compromise on these tax issues," and that he would be making “tough choices” in the coming days, including imposing new tax hikes on U.S. corporations, raising the corporate tax rate to 25 percent from 15 percent, and trimming spending on military equipment.
“We have reached an impasse on the tax issue,” said a spokesman for Geithner.
As such, both the president and Speaker Boehner are now left with few options for averting a fiscal cliff that, if not resolved, will come into effect on Jan. 1.
In the meantime, Boehner’s party will face pressure to do a lot of talking in the coming days, but without making much progress toward resolving a number of other issues, such as the debt ceiling, health care, immigration and the budget.
According to the Journal, the GOP was expected to focus on other issues than tax policy. In particular, White House aides are expected to be pushing for changes to the 2010 healthcare law, the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, that have yet to be approved. The Affordable Care Act would take effect in the first quarter of next year.
Meanwhile, Speaker Boehner has no plans to let the House leadership focus on other policy debates.
The House Democratic Caucus also released its own report on the tax issue. The report suggests that the House GOP is likely to make changes to the tax code on several fronts, including increasing rates on certain middle-class taxpayers in exchange for new deductions, simplifying the code to provide Americans greater certainty in how they can afford their taxes, and dropping the income thresholds for individual tax rates.
Other measures are also possible that are not currently part of the White House’s proposal.

Title: With Abortion in the Spotlight, a Challenge for Romney
Summary:
As the presidential campaign of one of the front-running candidates of the GOP reaches the halfway point, the party establishment is facing a difficult dilemma on its platform as it seeks to turn the page on the sexual misconduct scandals that have enveloped the White House for weeks. The platform is a key step toward creating the campaign that will propel Mitt Romney from the campaign trail to the White House.
The party has made an effort to paint Mr. Romney as the candidate who will “change the way Washington works,” but as the primary season unfolds, it seems doubtful he will be able to avoid this crucial conversation.
The Republican Party has already chosen in the last several weeks to move off its core message about jobs and the economy. The convention is intended to return the campaign’s message to one of how Mr. Romney will get the nation’s economy back on track.

Summary:
Mitt Romney is calling on Rep. Todd Akin (R-Mo.) to step aside in an interview with Sean Hannity on Tuesday. The Republican presidential candidate spoke of the need to focus on the future, not on the past, in an interview with Hannity on Tuesday.
Akin had vowed to remain in the race, and has now decided that he will not step aside in the state senate race. The Republican National Committee is hoping that the party would keep Akin in the race for the foreseeable future. Romney has been called to step down from the race if the current campaign doesn't turn out to be successful.
Akin's latest remarks suggest the former Missouri congressman has changed his opinion about the Republican Party and its candidate. Romney has accused the Republican candidate of "caving in to the power of big money" and "running from the center" because he refuses to consider a "real" alternative, namely Sarah Palin.
This statement by Romney is reminiscent of the words spoken by the former Massachusetts governor in 1999 in which he warned that Republicans are going to lose the next presidential election because the party has become so out of touch with the electorate.
Meanwhile, Paul Ryan's former political adviser Steve Schmidt has declared that the Republican National Committee (RNC) chairman has no intention of keeping Akin in the race for the foreseeable future.
Akin is the first GOP politician to say publicly that he intends to step down, but others have vowed to stay in the race.
Akin told Fox News Sunday that he is still willing to stay in the race if the current campaign doesn't work. He also admitted that he and the campaign need to "go deeper" in order to find a way to appeal to a large number of voters. Title: Romney calls on Rep. Akin to drop Senate bid over 'rape' comments
Summary:

Akin, who initially faced backlash for suggesting women could sue their attackers in court to get damages, said this after five different Missouri Republican senators, as well as the head of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, released their personal views on whether or not to support his campaign.
The Republican Party has tried to hold Akin out as a principled candidate, but the party has struggled to win over his conservative backers since they came to see the congressman's comments as a challenge to their political values. The party's senior leadership also refused to defend him on the air Monday, after some on the right complained the candidate's remarks weren't the focus of the evening.
Akin did not apologize for his original comments. He told KTVI Monday that the party should stand behind him for the job, but that the party should make some changes. "We would have a president who is fair and gets the job done," he said.
The Missouri Republican party didn't say whether they have any plans to do so, but it did say in a statement that the party has changed its policies on sexual harassment to protect women. The party added in the statement: "The Missouri Republican Party will always stand for Missouri's women and all women, and will not tolerate any effort to denigrate or harm women, no matter how heinous."

"I've repeatedly said I don't question the president's faith," Santorum told host Bob Schieffer, denying what some have said was a signal that Santorum had challenged the legitimacy of Obama's Christianity.
"I've repeatedly said that I believe the president's Christian -- he says he's Christian. But I am talking about his worldview, the way he addresses problems in this country, and they're different than most people view it in America."

Title: Donald Trump Sworn In As 45th President
Summary:
The election season did not turn out to be a total disaster for Donald Trump.
He won the Republican nomination, though, while he trailed the Democratic nominee in many polls. But he also won a number of contests by a larger margin than that needed for the general election.
He did not win the presidency.
And he likely will not.
What he did achieve, by any measure, was an impressive showing in two key contests that helped him in the campaign.
Trump was able to expand his lead over Clinton in the latest RealClearPolitics average of national polls to roughly 3 to 1.
He had gained more than 4 million more votes from the Democrats’ losses in two previous general election contests, including Ohio.
In each of the three Republican-held Senate races, including those in Wisconsin and Nevada, Trump outpaced Clinton by more than 20,000 votes, helping his chances of winning all of them. In a number of state House races, Trump outpaced his Democratic opponent by more than 20,000 votes.
The third way in which Trump’s election came close to defeating a Democratic opponent was his stunning victory in Florida, which cost Clinton a narrow margin in many polls.
In the last quarter of the election, Trump led the poll in a handful of races by more than 10,000 votes. He ended up losing Florida by almost 20,000 votes.
One could argue, though, that it may have been a little bit of a wash that he lost Florida, too, because in the final five days the lead that he had built up through the end of November gradually faded, giving Clinton the edge that she needed to prevail.
Clinton has built her case for the presidency in a way that contrasts sharply with the Republican critique of her campaign.
She argues that she has worked hard to make herself the best candidate, the candidate she can best beat the president, not just the next election. Her campaign has emphasized the need for her to highlight her record and her message, to highlight the economic progress she has overseen.
“I believe that it is imperative that the American people, particularly the people of Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Florida understand the real record that this candidate has put forward,” Clinton said in her concession speech on Thursday. “That record, that vision, that focus on making our country great again, should serve as a powerful counterpoint for the attacks that have been directed at me and at all of us for a long time.”

Title: Trump Calls Elephant Trophy Hunting A 'Horror Show,' Says He's Unlikely To Allows Imports
Summary:
The FWS is considering removing an annual ban on importation of big game trophies and removing a prohibition on exporting “crowned and mounted head trophies” to the United States, according to a draft of a rule that would affect trophy imports from Zimbabwe and Zambia.
The draft rule, which is being circulated for public review, would be the first of several revisions to the 2014 Federal Crop Management Plan, which restricts imports of trophy animals from those two countries. The draft rule, due out for public comment, could make it easier for U.S. importers to comply with trade laws, according to people familiar with it. The draft would also remove a prohibition on exports of heads and crowns from Zimbabwe and Zambia.
“Crowned and mounted head trophies are used by the international community in many instances for cultural and entertainment value,” the draft said, “and there is no evidence that these animals are causing harm or suffering to any endangered species.” The FWS also said it plans to use a “robust process to remove the annual ban” in the future.
The draft, however, would lift the annual ban, saying the U.S. should consider “using the import ban to encourage other countries to conduct more robust efforts to address the conservation of all wildlife, including those listed in the 2014 CMP.”
The FWS has not finalized its decision whether to remove the trade restrictions, according to the people.
The draft says the import ban would remain in place for “at least four additional years.”
The FWS’s consultation process in drafting its draft is continuing, though it has not yet received public comments about the rule, the people said.
The FWS is not using the import ban in the CMP to encourage countries to improve efforts to save animals, but to avoid the need to wait until after trade restrictions are lifted, the people said.

President Trump’s decision to delay lifting the federal ban on trophies from African elephants and other big game is being viewed with dismay across the world — and in some quarters with suspicion.

In a tweet on Friday night, Trump said he decided to put the "big game trophy decision on hold.” The comment comes less than 48 hours after it was first announced that the Trump administration would reverse a 2014 ban made under President Obama on permits for elephant trophies from Zambia and Zimbabwe.

Secretary of the Interior Ryan Zinke echoed Trump's comment in his own tweet, saying that he and the president had spoken and "both believe that conservation & healthy herds are critical...the issuing of permits is put on hold..."

It was not immediately clear why Trump made the announcement, but it came on the same day as the top Republican on the House Foreign Affairs Committee called on the Trump administration to reverse its newly announced policy, labeling it the "wrong move at the wrong time."

California Rep. Ed Royce on Friday questioned the action because of concerns not only about African wildlife but U.S. national security, citing the political upheaval in Zimbabwe, where the longtime president was placed under house arrest this week by the military.

"The administration should withdraw this decision until Zimbabwe stabilizes," the committee chairman said in a statement. "Elephants and other big game in Africa are blood currency for terrorist organizations, and they are being killed at an alarming rate. Stopping poaching isn't just about saving the world's most majestic animals for the future — it's about our national security."

Royce said that when carefully regulated, conservation hunts could help the wildlife population, but "that said, this is the wrong move at the wrong time."

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service said in a written notice issued Thursday that permitting elephants from Zimbabwe and Zambia to be brought back as trophies will raise money for conservation programs. The change marks a shift in efforts to stop the importation of elephant tusks and hides, overriding a 2014 ban imposed by the Obama administration. The newly announced policy applies to the remains of African elephants killed between January 2016 and December 2018.

Title: Double-Dip Recession Possible Without Tax Deal, Obama's Top Economic Aide Warns
Summary:
A week after voters passed the largest tax cut in U.S. history, President Obama and House Republicans are working on a tax bill that they say is the most significant accomplishment yet, yet would cost more in tax revenue. If lawmakers can't come to an agreement within two weeks, the economy may stall out.
White House officials and analysts say the president and Republican leaders want to reach an agreement that would raise about $2.1 trillion in tax revenues over the next 10 years. The tax bill would add $1 trillion to the deficit over the same period.
Senate Republicans need 50 votes to pass the bill, but Democrats have vowed to filibuster the legislation because it would affect Medicare recipients and the poor.
The House passed the Senate bill on Nov. 5 with a vote of 227-202 and Vice President Biden signed it into law on Nov. 14.
The White House has said the compromise will be "the best" of any in its long history, and said the president's tax cuts are "deeply conservative and in the economic interests of the American people."
But Democratic and some GOP lawmakers say the tax bill will cost the United States more in taxes and revenues than they anticipated.
Congressman Bill Thomas, D-Calif., said the bill creates tax loopholes that "will do nothing to stimulate the economy."
The administration says the $1 trillion increase in revenue comes mostly from the estate tax, as well as new taxes on investment income and the sale of business property. A key part of the package also calls for the elimination of a deduction for business owners who own more than one home, but not for those who have more than one home that is investment property.
Obama signed the bill into law Dec. 2, 2007.

That would be better than the 12% that came before the recession.
Summers, who is also the president's top economic adviser, also suggested in the interview that the deal Obama struck on the tax rate cuts will also benefit more than just the middle class.

Title: Senate Republicans Vow to Block Dem Legislation Until Tax Cuts, Budget Pass
Summary:
Reid and Senate Republican leadership have set the table for a long-term stalemate unless they can produce tax-and-spending legislation to keep the government working and ensure the passage of a budget.  Republicans will keep up the pressure to block any bill that doesn't extend these tax cuts for everybody -- that is, until the chamber makes good on its pledge to extend them.
As we noted Wednesday, that could mean either a significant increase in the debt ceiling on Oct. 1, or nothing more than a continuation of government operations.  On the debt ceiling, we'll know what the Democrats are planning, because the House will have to raise it anyway, unless President Obama calls up the U.S. Senate and orders a special session.
The Senate is controlled by Democrats for the first time since 2006 -- and they've been re-elected.
Meanwhile, a bipartisan group of Senate Republicans is vowing to hold the chamber hostage unless a vote is taken to make the government pay the debt, and has started a campaign called The Senate Is a Big, Evil, Boring Place to Sit In and Do Nothing.
"We have a job to do for this country," said House Republican Leader John Boehner, R-Ohio. "And what we'll get is an empty seat."
If Republicans keep holding their collective breath, Democrats and the White House might be forced to start a new debate over the budget and taxes.  In a statement, Democrats would have a simple choice:  Vote for an increase in the debt ceiling and continue the government's operations, or vote to stop spending without raising the debt ceiling.  On the tax issue, the House may have to vote to raise taxes on millionaires and pass a proposal that eliminates or at least reduces the child tax credit.
In fact, it's not even clear where Democrats stand on the issue.  The White House won't put a penny of its own money into raising the debt ceiling.  And with Republican majorities in both the House and Senate, any tax-and-spending bill Democrats may produce would be a nonstarter.
The Senate's filibuster threat also could force the White House to seek more revenue on the revenue side.
As we wrote Tuesday, if the Senate doesn't produce a budget proposal on the debt ceiling before Oct. 1, the White House could agree to an automatic budget increase without a vote in the House.

Title: Senate Republicans Vow to Block Dem Legislation Until Tax Cuts, Budget Pass
Summary:
The lame-duck session in the Senate has been a series of standoffs in which Republicans have been the main threat to passage of any legislation until the tax and spending debates are resolved.  But that's likely not going to stop the next session.
Biden's strategy has been to try to push the party and the White House onto different tracks, hoping to create a two-party, bipartisanship situation in Washington that will make it impossible for either party to use the veto to block progress.  That's worked as part of a strategy that Obama has used to make his own legislative demands for the last two years.
Obama has often complained the lame-duck session was too "partisan," particularly since he doesn't have a Senate majority, and "there is no way to get legislation through."  But the fact the last two years have proven that the president is far more interested in passing than blocking legislation shows that the party isn't going to be deterred.
Biden's chief goal in this standoff is to force Republicans to either back a bill or at least not attack it as a partisan move.
Reid, meanwhile, said this week in a briefing with the Senate Judiciary Committee that the only way to get through a deadlocked Congress is to get the government moving, at least on some issues.
On other matters, Reid has said he's not "trying to impose a partisan agenda that's going to be too difficult to accomplish by the lame duck session."
"I'm not going to do that," he said.  "I'm just not going to do that, and the goal would be to help the country as we move forward to a functioning government, to help us create jobs and grow the economy."
Republicans have been pushing their own agenda for the lame duck, such as extending the tax cuts for everyone by a year, and they're hoping the administration will step on the gas and do something about those.
Biden has indicated he's willing to let Congress work on those other items without getting into a prolonged standoff with Republicans, although he hasn't ruled them out outright.
"I think the president has made it clear that they are doing everything possible to stall, stall, stall," said Sen. Joe Lieberman, D-Conn., a potential vice presidential candidate.
"And I've made it clear that, at the end of the day, that's what we're here to do."
But others are not so sure there's any real choice left.

Summary:
When a group of black elected officials is preparing to vote on health care legislation, a small but vocal group of tea partiers take to the streets to decry the health care bill. The protests and civil disobedience — with the help of the Secret Service — keep black legislators in line. The Tea Party members are arrested, thrown in jail and black Tea Party activists are banned from speaking in their communities. But the real battle is waging inside the Tea Party movement itself. And the N.A.A.C.P. is taking note.

The movement that inspired the Tea Party movement is a broad one that includes a significant number of African Americans, people of all races and ethnicities, young and old, Democrats and Republicans. Its origins predate the Tea Party by nearly half a century and the movement it inspired is the product of a time when black Americans were not as represented in government, the press and the law as today.
But the movement today is different in many ways and its leaders can be found in communities that have not experienced the civil rights era.

Tea Party movements have developed since the 1980s. The first was in the Deep South, in the American South and Mississippi. The second was in the mid-1990s in Washington, D.C. and northern Virginia.
The third was in North Carolina and Virginia during the 1990s in Washington, D.C., New York and Pennsylvania. The movement has spread to other communities and areas — New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Miami, Washington, D.C., Florida and North Carolina — and it continues.
By the time the presidential primaries began in 2008, the movement was well-established in many places, including parts of Tennessee, South Carolina, Texas and Louisiana.
But the movement is growing. The Tea Party movement was created in the spring of 2007. By September 2009, when President Obama and the Democratic Party gained control of the Congress, there were more than 50 active, well-organized tea party groups nationwide.

Title: Reid: Mosque Should Be Built Someplace Else
Summary:
There are three primary issues in this case: the mosque and its constitutionality, the legal status of the Cordoba House in the context of national security policy, and the broader implications of its status for U.S. alliances and relations with allies.
The mosque: What is a mosque?

In the wake of the terrorist attacks of 9/11 and the aftermath of the war on terror, more questions emerged than answers about the proper constitutionality and legal status of the Cordoba House. Many Americans were angry that the project was allowed to proceed in its current location in Manhattan, a location that had long been a favorite of the New York Post's and the local paper's editorial boards and was chosen as a location for the proposed Islamic Cultural Center. But the mosque itself was not even questioned by many in Congress. So how did the Cordoba House get to this point?
A number of political actors were at the center of this saga. In 2005, David Wurmser, the Democratic chairman of the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee, began a fierce battle with Rep. Louise Slaughter of New York in an attempt to block a bill intended to "reform" the process for the building of mosques. While the House passed the bill in 2007, it went nowhere in the Senate. Steele is a relatively young and wealthy businessman who has come out as a gay man in his late 30s, a marriage he and his partner are now raising their two sons in. Steele's time as chairman of the RNC has been relatively short-lived, and his early departure would be a clear signal that he is ready to run for re-election. Many in the party have been growing increasingly dissatisfied with Steele's direction under his new leadership.
Many other Republicans say they are growing increasingly tired of the increasingly contentious, often combative and often fractious relationship between Steele and RNC Political Director and Chief Operating Officer Ed Gillespie, in particular. In fact, this past week has seen the announcement that Steele will take on a newly created role as a consultant for the RNC's political operations.
Another possibility is that Steele will run for reelection as a Democrat. While most GOP insiders are reluctant to speculate on the party's future path, it is still entirely possible for a Democrat to make a run for the party chair, as Republicans remain divided in their ranks on a host of issues. However, with the RNC split between conservatives and progressives, it would not be a surprise for Steele to consider a Democrat as his running mate.
Regardless of the eventual decision, Steele is the most recent high-profile RNC official to be openly gay. And yet, unlike many in the GOP, he is not alone among RNC Republicans in being openly gay. At this point, Steele has not publicly expressed a gay position on the subject. And it is possible that his decision to enter the race would signal that he has changed his mind on being gay.
But Steele is far from being the first RNC official to publicly affirm his sexual orientation. Many Republicans and right wingers are adamantly opposed to gay rights and the homosexual agenda, and there has been a noticeable increase in anti-gay rhetoric from conservative politicians in recent years. Scott Walker, a non-issue.

Summary:
Conservatives don't need a big tent. They just need a little more time.
The CPAC event, to the extent it did so, was about what Beck considered a lack of tent-pitching. Instead of taking the typical conservative road of being an out-of-power, out-the-gate politician, Beck was making a play for a political center ground.
In a speech so packed with ideas, the conservative commentator-turned-president seemed to take the long view. "For me, the American Dream isn't in the cities, but it is in the suburbs," he declared. "And in the suburbs, where I went to college, I didn't get a college education, but I am an American."
That statement may have seemed like a manifesto, but the way Beck was saying it -- with a glance at his audience -- may have been the same for most of the audience. The words "we," "my" and "your" were spoken much more often than "me," "our" and "yours." But he also sounded like a man who wasn't ready for his own party's future and instead would simply accept its present.
"You've got to give them time," Beck said to the GOP audience.
If past is prologue, then there's little hope of the GOP doing anything different this time around. In fact, it's clear that the party was not ready for this kind of out-of-power moment, and not willing to compromise its own principles. The last word in Beck's speech, before his appeal to the conservative grassroots, belonged to a man who seemed willing to sell out even the GOP's most faithful members.

Summary:
Trump administration announced Friday it has declared an emergency on the southern border with Mexico in an effort to divert money from federal health and other spending programs. Trump has used his executive authority under the National Emergencies Act, which authorizes him to declare emergencies, to divert funds from one program into another. The so-called "HR 1" measure embraced by House Democrats aims to curb big money in politics, make it easier to vote and bolster election security. It institutes a public financing system for congressional campaigns, requires presidential candidates to disclose tax returns and makes Election Day a federal holiday.

Title: Trump’s immigration offer brings sharp reactions from Dems and GOP
Summary:
President Trump's immigration compromise package to end the partial government shutdown drew sharp reactions from Democratic and Republican lawmakers alike.
In a televised White House address on Saturday afternoon, Trump offered Democrats a three-year extension of protections for 700,000 Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients, in exchange for the $5.7 billion he has been seeking for a barrier along the nation's southern border with Mexico.
“Our immigration system should be a source of pride... not a source of shame as it is all over the world,” Trump said in his plea.
The president's proposal was met with disdain from an array of top Democratic lawmakers. Many used the same language in their critiques, accusing Trump of holding the government and federal workers "hostage."
House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., tweeted, “What we didn’t hear from the President was any sympathy for the federal workers who face so much uncertainty because of the chaos of the #TrumpShutdown.”
Before Trump made his announcement, Pelosi had called his anticipated proposal “a non-starter.”
“For one thing, this proposal does not include the permanent solution for the Dreamers and TPS recipients that our country needs and supports.”
For his part, Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, called Trump's proposal "one-sided and ineffective."
“It's clear the President realizes that by closing the government and hurting so many American workers and their families, he has put himself and the country in an untenable position. Unfortunately, he keeps putting forward one-sided and ineffective remedies. There's only one way out: open the government, Mr. President, and then Democrats and Republicans can have a civil discussion and come up with bipartisan solutions."
Schumer, D-N.Y., concluded, "It was the President who single-handedly took away DACA and TPS protections in the first place – offering some protections back in exchange for the wall is not a compromise but more hostage taking."
House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer shared a similar sentiment, urging Trump and Sen. Mitch McConnell to "stop holding government hostage and end the shutdown" immediately.
“The president must stop holding government hostage and end the shutdown so federal employees can get back to work serving the American people. There is no reason for Americans to be shut out of work and without a paycheck while negotiations take place on the best way to secure our borders,” he said.

Title: Trump Declares National Emergency To Fund U.S.-Mexico Border Wall
Summary:
President Donald Trump on Friday declared a national emergency at the southern U.S. border in an effort to unilaterally seize funding to begin building his long-promised wall between the U.S. and Mexico.
A senior administration official has since told reporters that Trump had not been briefed about the National Emergency, according to the New York Times.
“There is no national emergency at the southern border. No need for a national emergency,” the official said, adding that Trump had been talking to his advisers about the issue.
Trump, who was accompanied by parents of children killed by unauthorized immigrants, said he was declaring the national emergency for “virtual invasion purposes.” He didn’t explain the full scope of his remarks.
The declaration will give Trump a chance to reroute other government money to fund the project ― and set up a legal battle that could tie up his signature project for months or years.
To justify the wall, Trump repeatedly insisted criminals, gang members and drug traffickers were pouring over the border and that only a wall could stop them.
“We have far more people trying to get into our country today than probably ever before,” Trump said.
In fact, arrests for illegal border crossings are at their lowest levels since the 1970s. There were roughly 520,000 arrests for unauthorized border crossings last year, which is about one-third of the 1.6 million arrests that happened in 2000. Since 2014, a high proportion of those crossing have been Central American children and families seeking to make humanitarian claims such as asylum.
The total wall funding will now come to about $8 billion, partially approved by Congress but mostly by Trump alone. That will buy the administration some 234 miles of border wall, a senior administration official told reporters Friday.
The national emergency declaration will allow the Trump administration to use about $3.6 billion from Defense Department construction projects to build the wall, along with another $2.5 billion the department had allocated for counter-drug activities, acting White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney told reporters.
The Trump administration also plans to take executive action to move about $200 million from the Department of Homeland Security and another $600 million from the Treasury Department’s asset forfeiture account.
None of the money will come from hurricane relief, Mulvaney said.

Summary:
After weeks of negotiations, the president of the United States agreed to use national emergency powers to get $5.7 billion to build his wall and then a federal judge ruled in his favor, halting the White House’s effort to get the funding to begin construction. The president then declared a national emergency on Friday morning to spend the funds, using his executive authority to create a legal barrier for Congress to fund the project.

The legal battle could last months or years
After being granted the authority to declare the emergency, Trump began spending the $1.375 billion.
The money will be used by the Customs and Border Protection agency, which has been fighting a lawsuit against the president since he announced a temporary ban on people seeking asylum at the southern border, the Los Angeles Times reports.
As the suit was about to proceed before being thrown out, however, a federal judge in Los Angeles on Thursday rejected Trump’s claim to the funds. He said the president had no authority to declare the emergency and that the move violated the Constitution’s Emoluments Clause.
In the ruling, the judge noted that the law specifically prohibits any federal funds from benefiting from the emoluments clause because the Constitution is not written in a way to cover the president’s use of his power. He said a ruling from the state’s highest court in New York ― the Second Circuit Court of Appeals ― could have potentially “saved” the president’s declaration.
The judge, Maureen O’Connor, said she is unsure what she could do to remedy Trump’s violation and warned that the president’s executive actions are legally questionable.
“Congressional appropriation of funds for this purpose is unquestionably the law of the land. It is a constitutional duty of the federal government to obey that congressional statute and to appropriate federal funds to carry out that duty,” she said.
The president called the ruling “a victory for the people of the United States” and added that the president “just made a legal decision.”
The ruling is likely to fuel the president’s efforts to get Congress to allow him to use another federal appropriation.

Title: House Democrats Pass Landmark Campaign Finance And Voting Rights Reform Bill
Summary:
Democratic leaders spent years crafting an ambitious reform agenda, including the For The People Act. Today, Democrats successfully passed the bill with a vote of 218-194. The bill is the culmination of that effort, and it is a big win for voters across the country and for democracy.
How it Works
The Democrats’ bill would dramatically expand voting access, create publicly funded House elections and strengthen the transparency of money in politics. To learn more, read Democracy in Action: A roadmap to a healthy democracy.
Key provisions:
Voting access
The bill establishes nonpartisan elections for the House and Senate, with nonpartisan election managers. Voters would be given the option to select “election winners” that would ensure that all candidates compete on a level playing field with the top two or three candidates. This change will provide more opportunity for voters to choose candidates they can trust. The bill also requires voter registration, enabling tens of millions of Americans who are not registered to cast ballots in their state.
The bill also addresses “voter fraud,” by requiring the state secretary of state to issue a statement to Congress every year that states if there is a voter fraud conviction, the state’s secretary of state would be liable for the cost of the court-ordered removal of the voter. The bill also requires public information on elections, including the list of ballot initiatives that have passed by popular vote and a description of the ballot questions and procedures.
Voting Rights
The bill protects individuals’ First Amendment right to free speech and press, allowing for public debate on campaign finance and the role of money in politics. It also strengthens state and federal laws that protect people’s voting rights.
Transparency
The bill establishes a public filing requirement. Currently, the House and Senate must file reports with the Office of the Clerk with the names and identifying information on all campaign donors, as well as the names and addresses of any public officials who voted for a particular candidate. The act will increase the transparency of campaign finance and increase public oversight of government.
Elections
The bill provides for an elected House and Senate to conduct elections on a national basis. To ensure impartiality, the House and Senate will appoint nonpartisan election managers, with the managers responsible to the House and Senate. The managers will then distribute the results of all votes to the public.

Title: House Democrats Pass Landmark Campaign Finance And Voting Rights Reform Bill
Summary:
The For the People Act, which passed 234-193, was Democrats’ top priority upon winning control of the House in the 2018 elections. It would dramatically expand voting access, create publicly funded House elections, enhance the transparency of money in politics, restore voting rights to millions of ex-felons, strengthen executive branch ethics law and end partisan gerrymandering.
The bill aims to answer rising attacks on voting rights from courts and politicians across the country, and also to stem the increasing inequality of campaign funding by empowering small donors with matching contributions from public funds, among many other things.
The For The People Act “takes power from the elites, special interests and the 1 percent and gives it to the American people,” Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.) said. “This vote is an opportunity to be on the right side of history,” Rep. John Lewis (D-Ga.) said. “If not us, then who? If not now, then when?”
House passage of the legislation is the result of a long collaborative process by the Democratic Party to prioritize campaign finance and voting rights reforms. The party’s Democracy Reform Task Force, endorsed by Pelosi and led by Rep. John Sarbanes (D-Md.), worked with lawmakers both old and new to bring together legislative ideas and craft them into a coherent package.
Much of this work was begun while Democrats languished in the House minority. As a possible victory in the 2018 elections loomed, they made it clear that the reforms would be their No. 1 priority. This mission was driven not just by party leaders, but also by the candidates who would ultimately deliver Democrats their first majority in the House in eight years.
One-hundred candidates, including those who won their 2018 races, signed a letter to Pelosi and other congressional leaders demanding the reforms be the first order of business. Many cited the endemic corruption of money in politics as a top complaint they heard on the campaign trail from constituents.

Title: Trump Associate Roger Stone Indicted In Mueller Investigation
Summary:
Roger Stone, a longtime adviser to the Trump campaign who is a Russian spy and has close ties to the Russian government, pleaded not guilty on Monday to seven charges. Stone has said he was in regular contact with senior members of Trump’s campaign, including his presidential campaign chairman Paul Manafort and Manafort associate Rick Gates, before, during and after the 2016 election. Stone’s lawyer Grant Smith said in a statement that he believed Stone could be exonerated on any of the charges, and said the charges were “a clear attempt to silence Roger.”
Stone faces 14 charges that include bribery, witness tampering and obstruction of an official proceeding. The charges could result in life in prison, a maximum sentence for the maximum amount of time.
If convicted on all 14 charges, Stone could have to serve at least 17 years before receiving any release date from prison.
The charges are based on texts and other documents that Stone sent and received with his former mistress, Stormy Daniels, to a former business partner, who is a lawyer for Trump, according to Smith.
Smith said Stone’s indictment “is an attempt by the government to take down the whole Trump presidency based on lies and misrepresentations,” including the lies and misrepresentations related to the 2016 election.
The charges also accuse Stone of lying about discussions he had with a Russian spy to gather information on Trump, who is not a citizen of the United States. Stone denies having contacts with the Russians, and the Justice Department has not said whether it will seek to extradite Stone for his potential cooperation.
The indictment states that Stone was “aware that it was the Russians” who engaged in the hacking of Democratic emails, and said “that it was the Russians who were responsible for leaking this information to the public.”

Summary:

Federal authorities made an arrest on Friday in connection with the nationwide bombing campaign against outspoken critics of President Trump, a significant breakthrough in a case that has gripped the country in the days leading up to the midterm elections.
A law enforcement official identified the suspect as Cesar Sayoc Jr., 56, of Aventura, Fla., just north of Miami.

Title: Texas Rep. Blake Farenthold resigns from Congress
Summary:
Blake Farenthold accused of multiple sexual harassment allegations and lewd comments and inappropriate comments about staff members

U.S. Rep. Blake Farenthold resigned from Congress on Friday, following multiple allegations of sexual harassment, misconduct and inappropriate behavior.
Farenthold, R-Texas, had previously announced that he would not seek re-election in the 2018 midterm election, when reports of sexual misconduct first surfaced.
“While I planned on serving out the remainder of my term in Congress, I know in my heart it’s time for me to move along and look for new ways to serve,” Farenthold said in a statement Friday evening, noting he sent a letter to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to tell him about his resignation, effective at 5 p.m.
“It’s been an honor and privilege to serve the constituents of Texas’ 27th Congressional District. I would like to thank my staff both in Washington and Texas for all of their hard work on behalf of our constituents. I would also like to thank my family for their unwavering support and most importantly the people that elected me,” Farenthold said. “Leaving my service in the House, I’m able to look back at the entirety of my career in public office and say that it was well worthwhile.”
Farenthold was sued by his former aide, Lauren Greene, in 2014, alleging a hostile work environment, gender discrimination and retaliation. Among other things, Greene claimed Farenthold asked her for a threesome. She sued him and was paid $84,000 from a public fund on behalf of Farenthold for a sexual harassment claim.
Farenthold pledged to repay the $84,000 in taxpayer money spent to settle the claim.
Farenthold’s former communications director, Michael Rekola, also described in detail the congressman’s alleged abusive behavior toward staff members, which ranged from making sexually graphic jokes to verbally abusing his aides.
Other staffers accused Farenthold of routinely commenting on the size of women’s breasts and making jokes about being on “redhead patrol” because he was attracted to women with red hair.

In his written argument, Boutrous called for Wal-Mart to be held in civil contempt of court.

Title: AARP Willing To Negotiate On Social Security Retirement Age
Summary:
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday morning that AARP, one of the most influential lobbying groups in Washington, was softening its opposition to cutting retirement benefits.
AARP originally pushed back against the newspaper's story.
"Stay tuned -- our position has not changed on Social Security," an AARP spokeswoman said in an email to HuffPost.
AARP legislative policy director David Certner said on CNN Friday that "there was some miscommunication with the Wall Street Journal story."
But then Certner acknowledged that AARP believes the program needs to be changed.
"Everybody knows we need to look at a package of different changes to Social Security to make it strong for the long term," he said. "The reality is, we have more people older and who are living longer, so we need to make changes. Everybody recognizes that. And we're certainly willing to talk about a package of changes that will keep Social Security strong."
He suggested raising the age at which retirees can receive full benefits -- currently, 66 years old -- would be on the table even though doing so represents "a massive benefit cut for people."
The 37 million-member lobbying powerhouse launched a national ad campaign Thursday warning members of Congress not to reduce benefits for recipients of Social Security and Medicare.
Jonathan Cowan, president of centrist think tank Third Way, hailed AARP's apparent reversal, per the Journal story.
"Today marks a watershed moment in American politics," Cowan said. "For decades, AARP has stood against any substantial changes to Social Security. Now that they have opened the door to reform, it is time for lawmakers to walk through it."
Yet AARP reassured labor groups that it had not changed its position on Social Security, labor officials told HuffPost.
"The AARP has a history of division between the top folks and their base on these issues. The top folks like to be in the inside game," one union official said. "But they are walking backwards now."
The official said that he and other opponents of benefit cuts had been told that AARP's "longstanding position" hadn't changed, but there was some uncertainty about what that position actually is.
If AARP is open to reducing benefits, it would be a major boost for Social Security reformers who say the program is too generous and therefore unaffordable.

AARP said Friday that it doesn't expect to significantly alter its policy regarding the issue. "This is something that was discussed in the past, but the AARP has not changed its position," said AARP's chief executive officer A. Barry Rand, a former lobbyist and congressional aide. "We'll look at these ideas on their merits but not make a decision at this time."
RAND said that the group still strongly believes in Social Security as it currently functions and it "will always look to strengthen Social Security for the long-term," per the statement from Rand.
The AARP leader noted that the organization's senior members do indeed want to see the program strengthened, but it has never suggested that it is open to any proposal from Congress or a Republican president that aims to reduce benefits and make Social Security solvent.
"You would have a lot of members who would like to make Social Security solvent and they're not going to vote for us," Rand said. "They want their benefits and they're not going to go for that."
"You're very much in the majority on this," a spokesman for the AARP, Michael Heinisch, told the Associated Press, referring to a report from the nonpartisan Pew Charitable Trusts saying that AARP members are on the fence about the issue.

"It's up to Congress to look at what they want to do," Rand said. "We want them to provide for seniors, but we want them to take care of what we have."

Title: AARP Open to Social Security Cuts
Summary:
The Social Security system is facing multiple threats and challenges, and the aging of the population is only one of the risks. At the same time, Social Security benefits that provide significant financial security for retirees are under attack in the budgeting process, and a variety of stakeholders have called for measures to address the problems at the system’s core. AARP, the powerful lobbying organization for older Americans, has become one of those stakeholders.
The group, which is considered a key player in Social Security reform efforts, is well-aware of the dangers that could threaten current retirees, and the need for additional revenue to fund the system’s future growth. AARP, founded in 1965, counts some of the largest foundations in the country among its members and has a vast network of members around the country and the world.
Social Security is generally considered the poster child for a program that’s in deep trouble, and AARP’s stance on Social Security is particularly significant because of the organization’s position on Medicare, prescription drugs, and other programs affecting older Americans.
By itself, AARP has not sought to play a leading role in changing Social Security. However, the organization’s recent statements reflect a realization that Congress and the administration may be looking for a more proactive approach than AARP was willing to take last year when it first emerged with a proposal to reduce benefits to current retirees by 25 percent.
The change was driven by conservative Republicans, including Rep. Ron Paul (R-TX), who proposed eliminating the cap on benefits, which was scheduled to increase from current levels of $2,000 to $4,500, for all recipients.
But the plan was opposed by both Democrats and the unions that represent Social Security recipients. AARP has been working on a compromise that would have cut benefits for current recipients to $1,000, about the same as the current system, and increase the cap on benefits to $10,000 for future recipients.
But instead of meeting the bipartisan expectations, AARP decided to wait until next year, when a major fiscal update to Social Security would be passed in Congress, to take a more forceful stance.
“Last year, AARP made it clear that they were willing to work with both sides of the aisle,” a senior AARP official said, “and now it is clear that in 2010, we will not be playing a partisan role.”
AARP’s official stance toward Social Security cuts remains unchanged.
